description: Plan-domain fixture: 'Add OAuth2 social login to existing email-only auth'. 6 findings covering finding/missing/perspective categories. Used to validate that reviewer/critic agents apply plan-specific Phase 4 (Key Assumptions / Pre-Mortem / Dependency Audit / Ambiguity Scan / Rollback Analysis) and the executor/stakeholder/skeptic perspectives.

findings.summary: Session migration mid-flight unspecified — existing email-session users during deployment may lose state
findings.explanation: The plan switches the auth middleware from email-only to dual email+OAuth. It does not specify what happens to users with active email-based sessions when the new code deploys: are sessions preserved, force-renewed, or dropped? An undocumented session-flush during deploy would log out every active user simultaneously. Pre-mortem: deploy at peak traffic → mass logout → support flood.

findings.summary: No rollback path defined if OAuth provider has an outage during cutover
findings.explanation: The plan assumes the OAuth provider is always available. There is no rollback procedure for: (a) provider outage during deployment, (b) provider deprecating the API version we depend on, (c) needing to disable OAuth for security reasons mid-flight. Standard pattern: feature flag + email-only fallback path that stays maintained for at least one quarter.

findings.summary: Token refresh strategy not addressed — OAuth2 access tokens expire and the plan does not specify the refresh flow
findings.explanation: OAuth2 access tokens typically expire in 1 hour. The plan describes the initial authorization code exchange but says nothing about: storing refresh tokens, automatic refresh before API calls, handling refresh failures (e.g., user revoked access). Without this, every OAuth user gets logged out after the first hour.

findings.summary: Account linking ambiguity unresolved — what if OAuth email matches an existing email-only account?
findings.explanation: If a user signs up via OAuth with an email that already has an email-only account, the plan does not specify whether to: (a) auto-link (security risk if OAuth-side email is unverified), (b) prompt user to link with email-side authentication, (c) treat as separate accounts. Each choice has very different UX and security implications. Ambiguity scan: two competent developers will pick different defaults.

findings.summary: Stakeholder perspective: success criterion is a vanity metric (OAuth signups grow), not a meaningful outcome (auth friction drops)
findings.explanation: The plan defines success as 'X% of new signups use OAuth within Q1'. This is measurable but vanity — adoption rate does not prove auth friction was actually reduced (users may still abandon, just earlier). A stakeholder-perspective review would push for: signup completion rate change, time-to-first-action change, or support-ticket volume change.

findings.summary: Executor perspective: ownership of provider-side configuration not assigned — who rotates secrets, monitors deprecation notices?
findings.explanation: The plan delivers OAuth integration but does not name the team responsible for ongoing provider-side operations: rotating client-side secrets quarterly, watching the provider's deprecation calendar, responding to provider security advisories. Executor-perspective question: 'Who do I escalate to when the provider sends a breaking-change notice?' Currently unanswered.
